questions.q: A 64-tooth gear drives a 176-tooth gear. What is the gear ratio?
questions.explain: 176 ÷ 64 = 2.75, so the small gear turns 2.75 times for each turn of the big gear: a 2.75:1 reduction.

questions.q: A small gear drives a big gear (a reduction). The big gear turns...
wrong: Faster, with more torque
Faster, with less torque
At the same speed, with the same torque
questions.explain: A reduction trades speed for strength: the output turns slower but twists harder.

questions.q: What does the 1:3.2 overdrive kit do to the servo's output?
questions.correct: Turns it 3.2× farther and faster, with less torque
wrong: Makes it 3.2× stronger but 3.2× slower to turn
Lets it spin forever like a continuous servo
Makes it hold its angle 3.2× more accurately
questions.explain: Overdrive is the opposite of a reduction: more speed and travel, less torque. The Axon MAX has torque to spare.

questions.q: Why can't a positional servo spin forever?
questions.correct: Its built-in sensor only covers a limited angle range
wrong: FTC rules ban servos from turning more than once
Its wires would twist off inside the case
It would overheat after one full turn
questions.explain: A positional servo knows its angle from an internal sensor, and that sensor only covers about 350° on the Axon MAX. Past that, it stops.

questions.q: A continuous-rotation servo can spin forever. Why don't we use one for the turret?
questions.correct: You control its speed, not its angle, so it can't hold an aim
wrong: It's far too weak to move a turret with a shooter on it
It only spins in one direction, so the turret can't come back
It needs a motor port instead of a servo port
questions.explain: Continuous mode gives up knowing the angle. For aiming we need setPosition() to drive to an angle and hold it.

questions.q: With NO overdrive, how far could the 350° servo turn the 2.75:1 turret?
wrong: About 962°
About 350°
About 407°
questions.explain: 350 ÷ 2.75 ≈ 127°, only about a third of a circle. That's the problem the overdrive solves.

questions.q: With the 1:3.2 overdrive, how far can the turret turn at the servo's full signal?
wrong: About 127°
About 1,120°
About 3,080°
questions.explain: 350 × 3.2 = 1,120° out of the gearbox, then ÷ 2.75 ≈ 407° at the turret: more than a full circle.

questions.q: Why does the lesson use about 367° instead of 407°?
questions.correct: The Control Hub's default servo signal reaches about 90% of the range
wrong: The turret's bearing adds friction that eats about 40°
The gears lose teeth over time, so we leave extra room
FTC rules limit turrets to one full turn plus a bit
questions.explain: The servo's full 350° needs a 500–2500 µs signal; the hub's default is narrower, so you get about 90% of the travel.

questions.q: Using turret angle = (position − 0.5) × 367°, where does position 0.6 point?
wrong: About 37° to the right
About 220° to the left
Straight forward
questions.explain: (0.6 − 0.5) × 367 ≈ 37°. Positive angles are to the left (counter-clockwise).

questions.q: Which servo position points the turret straight forward?
questions.explain: We assemble the turret with the servo at 0.5, so the middle of the range is forward and there's equal travel each way.

questions.q: To aim the turret at 0° with no limits, what position would you send?
questions.explain: position = 0.5 + angle ÷ 367°. For 0°, that's just 0.5.

questions.q: Why do we send the servo to 0.5 BEFORE meshing the turret gears?
questions.correct: So 0.5 means forward, with equal travel both ways
wrong: Because the gears only mesh when the servo is powered
So the servo is at its strongest when meshing
Because 0.5 is the only legal starting position
questions.explain: Centering first lines up the code's middle with the turret's forward direction, so you can swing equally left and right.

questions.q: What happens to a positional-servo turret when you press INIT?
questions.correct: It jumps to its starting position right away
wrong: Nothing, until the driver presses START
It slowly searches for the forward direction
It spins one full turn to calibrate itself
questions.explain: As soon as the code sends a position, the servo drives there. Keep hands clear of the turret at INIT.

questions.q: Why does the Turret code clamp the position between MIN_POS and MAX_POS?
questions.correct: So the turret can't swing far enough to wrap and pull the wires
wrong: So the servo doesn't overheat from moving too far
Because positions outside 0.15–0.85 are illegal in FTC
So the turret always points toward the goal
questions.explain: More than a full circle of travel can wrap cables. Software limits keep the turret inside a safe range.

questions.q: Why put the Axon MAX on a servo power injector?
questions.correct: It can draw up to 4 A, more than the hub's servo ports like to supply
wrong: Servo power injectors make the servo turn 3.2× farther
Without one, the servo can only run in continuous mode
It's needed to send the servo its position signal
questions.explain: A strong servo under load can brown out the hub's servo power. The injector feeds it extra power.

questions.q: Holding D-pad left calls nudgeLeft() every loop. How does the turret move?
questions.correct: A small fixed step each loop, adding up to a smooth swing
wrong: One big jump to the far left limit
Faster the harder you press the button
It stays still until you let go of the button
questions.explain: A D-pad button is just on or off, so each loop adds the same NUDGE_STEP. Dozens of loops a second add up to a smooth swing.

questions.q: The turret swings RIGHT when you hold D-pad left. What's the simplest fix?
questions.correct: Reverse the servo's direction in the code
wrong: Take the turret apart and flip the gears over
Swap the servo cable to a different port
Change the overdrive kit to a 3.2:1 reduction
questions.explain: Meshing gears flip direction. servo.setDirection(Servo.Direction.REVERSE) flips it back in software.

questions.q: What does nudgeLeft() actually do?
questions.correct: Changes the position field; update() moves the servo
wrong: Moves the servo immediately, without update()
Waits until the turret has finished moving
Resets the turret back to forward
questions.explain: Like every subsystem command, it only changes the state. robot.update() calls the turret's update(), which sends the position to the servo.

questions.q: Why does the Turret code include a setAngle(degrees) method?
questions.correct: So auto-aim code can just say which angle to point at
wrong: Because the servo only understands degrees, not positions
So the driver can type an angle on the gamepad
To make the D-pad nudges more accurate
questions.explain: Later, Limelight or odometry code will work out the angle to the goal and call setAngle(). The turret does the position math.

questions.q: How could odometry help the turret aim at the goal?
questions.correct: Use the robot's pose and the goal's spot to compute the angle
wrong: Odometry pods can see the goal's AprilTag
Odometry measures the turret's gear teeth
Odometry spins the turret until the shots go in
questions.explain: The Pinpoint knows where the robot is. With the goal's known position, Math.atan2 gives the direction to it, minus the robot's heading.
